replacement: 1. Breeding an animal that can make promises — is this not the very paradox of a task that nature has set itself with regard to man? Is it not the real problem of man? Anyone who can fully appreciate the force of forgetfulness, which works against it, will find it all the more remarkable that the problem has been largely solved. Forgetfulness is not simply a vis inertiæ, as the superficial believe. It is rather an active power of obstruction, positive in the strictest sense of the word. It is the reason why nothing we live through, experience or take into ourselves enters consciousness while we digest it (we might call this psychic absorption), any more than the whole manifold process of our physical nutrition, the so-called "incorporation," does. The doors and windows of consciousness are shut for a time. We are relieved of the clamor of alarms and skirmishes with which our subconscious world of servant organs works in mutual co-operation and antagonism. There is a little quiet, a little tabula rasa of consciousness, to make room again for the new, and above all for the nobler functions and functionaries: room for government, foresight, predetermination (for our organism is built on an oligarchic model). This, as I have said, is the use of active forgetfulness. It is a very sentinel and nurse of psychic order, repose and etiquette; and it shows at once why there can be no happiness, no gladness, no hope, no pride, no real present, without forgetfulness. If this preventive apparatus is damaged and broken in a man, he is like a dyspeptic, and more than like one — he can "get rid of" nothing. But this very animal, who must be forgetful, and in whom forgetfulness is a force and a form of robust health, has bred for himself an opposing power, a memory, with whose help forgetfulness is in certain cases held in check — namely in the cases where promises have to be made. So this memory is by no means a merely passive inability to get rid of an impression once made, nor merely the indigestion caused by a pledged word that one cannot dispose of. It is an active refusal to get rid of it, a continuing and a wish to continue what was once willed: an actual memory of the will. Between the original "I will," "I shall do," and the actual discharge of the will, its act, we can therefore easily interpose a world of new and strange circumstances, events and even acts of will, without snapping this long chain of the will. But what does all this presuppose? In order to regulate the future in this way, man must first have learnt, and learnt thoroughly, to distinguish necessitated from accidental events, to think causally, to see the distant as present and anticipate it, to fix with certainty what is the end and what the means to that end, and above all to reckon, to be able to calculate. Man must first have become thoroughly calculable, disciplined, necessitated, even in his own eyes and his own conception of himself, so that, like a man making a promise, he could guarantee himself as a future.

note: One question split into two; source has a single question.
replacement: 2. All this is simply the long history of the origin of responsibility. The task of breeding an animal that can make promises includes, as we have already seen, a more immediate task as its condition and preliminary: first to make man to a certain extent necessitated, uniform, like among his like, regular and therefore calculable. What I have called the "morality of custom" (cp. Dawn of Day, Aphs. 9, 14, and 16) was an immense work: man's actual work on himself during the longest period of the human race, his whole prehistoric work. This work finds its meaning and its great justification (in spite of all its innate hardness, despotism, stupidity and idiocy) in this: with the help of the morality of customs and of social strait-waistcoats, man was made genuinely calculable. But suppose we stand at the end of this colossal process, at the point where the tree finally ripens its fruit and society and its morality of custom at last bring to light what they were only the means to. There we find, as the ripest fruit on its tree, the sovereign individual, who resembles only himself, who has got loose from the morality of custom: the autonomous "super-moral" individual (for "autonomous" and "moral" exclude each other) — in short, the man of the personal, long and independent will, who is able to promise. In him we find a proud consciousness, vibrating in every fibre, of what has at last been achieved and has come alive in him, a genuine consciousness of power and freedom, a feeling of human perfection in general. And this man who has grown to freedom, who is really able to promise, this lord of the free will, this sovereign — how can he fail to know how great his superiority is over everything that cannot bind itself by promises or be its own security, how great a trust, awe and reverence he awakens (he "deserves" all three), and that with this mastery over himself he is necessarily also given mastery over circumstances, over nature, over all creatures with shorter wills and less reliable characters? The "free" man, the owner of a long, unbreakable will, finds in this possession his standard of value. Looking out from himself upon others, he honors or he despises. Just as necessarily as he honors his peers, the strong and the reliable (those who can bind themselves by promises) — that is, everyone who promises like a sovereign, with difficulty, rarely and slowly, who is sparing with his trust but confers honor by the very act of trusting, who gives his word as something that can be relied on because he knows himself strong enough to keep it even in the teeth of disasters, even in the "teeth of fate" — so with equal necessity will he have the heel of his foot ready for the lean and empty jackasses who promise when they have no business to, and his rod of chastisement ready for the liar who already breaks his word at the very moment it is on his lips. The proud knowledge of the extraordinary privilege of responsibility, the consciousness of this rare freedom, of this power over himself and over fate, has sunk right down to his innermost depths and has become an instinct, a dominating instinct. What name will he give to it, to this dominating instinct, if he needs a word for it? There is no doubt about it: the sovereign man calls it his conscience.

3. His conscience? — One sees at once that the idea "conscience," which appears here in its supreme form, supreme almost to the point of strangeness, must already have a long history and evolution behind it. To be able to guarantee oneself with all due pride, and at the same time to say yes to oneself — that is, as has been said, a ripe fruit, but also a late fruit. How long this fruit had to hang sour and bitter on the tree! And for a still longer period there was not a glimpse of such a fruit to be had. No one had taken it on himself to promise it, although everything on the tree was quite ready for it and everything was maturing toward that very consummation. "How is a memory to be made for the man-animal? How is an impression to be fixed so deeply upon this ephemeral understanding, half dense and half silly, upon this incarnate forgetfulness, that it will stay permanently present?" One may imagine that this primeval problem was not solved with exactly gentle answers and gentle means. Perhaps there is nothing more awful and more sinister in the early history of man than his system of mnemonics. "Something is burnt in so that it stays in his memory: only what never stops hurting stays in his memory." This is an axiom of the oldest (unfortunately also the longest) psychology in the world. It might even be said that wherever solemnity, seriousness, mystery and gloomy colors are now found in the life of men and nations, there is some survival of that horror which was once the universal companion of all promises, pledges and obligations. The past, the past with all its length, depth and hardness, breathes on us and wells up in us again when we become "serious." Whenever man has thought it necessary to make a memory for himself, it has never happened without blood, tortures and sacrifice. The most dreadful sacrifices and forfeitures belong here (among them the sacrifice of the first-born), the most loathsome mutilations (for instance, castration), the most cruel rituals of all the religious cults (for all religions are really at bottom systems of cruelty) — all these things originate in that instinct which found in pain its most potent mnemonic. In a certain sense the whole of asceticism is to be ascribed to this. Certain ideas have to be made inextinguishable, omnipresent, "fixed," with the aim of hypnotizing the whole nervous and intellectual system through these "fixed ideas" — and the ascetic methods and modes of life are the means of freeing those ideas from competition with all other ideas, so as to make them "unforgettable." The worse man's memory was, the ghastlier the signs presented by his customs. The severity of the penal laws in particular gives a gauge of how hard man found it to conquer forgetfulness, and to keep a few primal postulates of social life present in the minds of those who were slaves of every momentary emotion and every momentary desire. We Germans certainly do not regard ourselves as an especially cruel and hard-hearted nation, still less as an especially casual and happy-go-lucky one. But one has only to look at our old penal ordinances to realize how much trouble it takes in the world to develop a "nation of thinkers" (I mean: the European nation that today shows the maximum of reliability, seriousness, bad taste and positiveness, and that on the strength of these qualities has a right to train every kind of European mandarin). These Germans used terrible means to make a memory for themselves, to master their rooted plebeian instincts and the brutal crudity of those instincts. Think of the old German punishments: stoning (as far back as the legend, the millstone falls on the head of the guilty man); breaking on the wheel (the most original invention and speciality of the German genius in the sphere of punishment); dart-throwing; tearing or trampling by horses ("quartering"); boiling the criminal in oil or wine (still practiced in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries); the highly popular flaying ("slicing into strips"); cutting the flesh out of the breast. Think also of the evil-doer smeared with honey and then exposed to the flies in a blazing sun. With the help of such images and precedents man finally kept in his memory five or six "I will nots," about which he had already given his promise so as to enjoy the advantages of society — and truly, with the help of this kind of memory man finally arrived at "reason"! Alas! Reason, seriousness, mastery over the emotions, all these gloomy, dismal things called reflection, all these privileges and pageantries of humanity: how dear is the price they have exacted! How much blood and cruelty lies at the foundation of all "good things"!

replacement: Have these current genealogists of morals ever allowed themselves even the vaguest notion, for instance, that the cardinal moral idea of "ought" originates in the very material idea of "owe"? Or that punishment developed as a retaliation absolutely independently of any prior assumption about the freedom or determination of the will? — And this to such an extent that a high degree of civilization was always necessary first, before the animal man could begin to make those much more primitive distinctions of "intentional," "negligent," "accidental," "responsible," and their contraries, and apply them in assessing punishment. That idea — "the wrong-doer deserves punishment because he might have acted otherwise" — is nowadays so cheap, obvious, natural and inevitable, and has had to serve as an illustration of how the sentiment of justice appeared on earth; yet in fact it is an exceedingly late, even refined, form of human judgment and inference, and to project it back to the beginning of the world is simply a clumsy violation of the principles of primitive psychology. Throughout the longest period of human history punishment was never based on the evil-doer's responsibility for his action, and was therefore not based on the assumption that only the guilty should be punished. On the contrary, punishment was inflicted for the same reason that parents punish their children even nowadays: out of anger at an injury suffered, an anger that vents itself mechanically on the author of the injury. But this anger is kept in bounds and modified by the idea that every injury has somewhere its equivalent price and can really be paid off, even if by means of pain to the author. Where has this ancient, deep-rooted and now perhaps ineradicable idea, the idea of an equivalence between injury and pain, drawn its strength? I have already revealed its origin: it lies in the contractual relationship between creditor and debtor, which is as old as the existence of legal rights at all, and which in its turn points back to the primary forms of purchase, sale, barter and trade.

note: "The realisation of these contractual relations" dropped as the subject.
replacement: 5. The realization of these contractual relations naturally arouses (as our previous remarks would lead us to expect) a great deal of suspicion and opposition toward the primitive society that made or sanctioned them. In this society promises will be made; in this society the aim is to give the promiser a memory; in this society, as we may suspect, there will be full scope for hardness, cruelty and pain. The "debtor," in order to inspire credit in his promise of repayment, in order to guarantee the earnestness and sanctity of his promise, in order to drill into his own conscience the duty, the solemn duty, of repayment, will pledge something he still possesses, something still in his power, under a contract with his creditor to cover the case of his not paying. He may pledge his life or his wife, or his freedom or his body (or, under certain religious conditions, even his salvation, his soul's welfare, even his peace in the grave; so in Egypt, where the corpse of the debtor found no rest from the creditor even in the grave — and from the Egyptian standpoint this peace was of particular importance). But above all the creditor has the power to inflict on the body of the debtor all kinds of pain and torture, for instance to cut off as much as seemed proportionate to the size of the debt. From this point of view precise schemes of valuation arose early and everywhere, often horrible in the minuteness and meticulousness with which they were applied: legally sanctioned valuations for individual limbs and parts of the body. I consider it already a progress, a proof of a freer, less petty and more Roman conception of law, when the Roman Code of the Twelve Tables decreed that it did not matter how much or how little the creditors cut off in such a case: "si plus minusve secuerunt, ne fraude esto." Let us make the logic of this whole process of equalization clear; it is strange enough. The equivalence is this: instead of an advantage that directly compensates for his injury (that is, instead of an equalization in money, lands or some kind of chattel), the creditor is granted, by way of repayment and compensation, a certain sensation of satisfaction. It is the satisfaction of being able to vent his power without any trouble on one who is powerless, the delight "de faire le mal pour le plaisir de le faire," the joy in sheer violence. This joy will be relished in proportion to the lowness and humbleness of the creditor's place in society, and it is quite apt to have the effect of the most delicious dainty, and even to seem a foretaste of a higher social position. Thanks to the punishment of the "debtor," the creditor shares in the rights of the masters. At last he too, for once, attains the edifying consciousness of being able to despise and ill-treat a creature as an "inferior" — or at any rate of seeing him despised and ill-treated, in case the actual power of punishing, the administration of punishment, has already been transferred to the "authorities." So the compensation consists in a claim on cruelty and a right to draw on it.

replacement: 7. Since I hold these thoughts, I am, let me say in parenthesis, fundamentally opposed to supplying our pessimists with fresh water for the discordant, groaning mills of their disgust with life. On the contrary, it should be shown specifically that at the time when mankind was not yet ashamed of its cruelty, life on earth was brighter than it is nowadays, when there are pessimists. The darkening of the heavens over man has always grown in proportion to the growth of man's shame before man. The tired pessimistic outlook, the mistrust of the riddle of life, the icy negation of disgusted ennui — none of these is a sign of the most evil age of the human race. Much rather do they first come to light, as the swamp-flowers they are, when the swamp they belong to comes into existence. I mean the diseased refinement and moralization thanks to which the "animal man" has at last learnt to be ashamed of all his instincts. On the road to angelhood (not to use a harder word in this context) man has developed that dyspeptic stomach and coated tongue which have made not only the joy and innocence of the animal repulsive to him, but life itself — so that sometimes he stands before his own self with stopped nostrils and, like Pope Innocent the Third, draws up a black list of his own horrors ("unclean generation, loathsome nutrition when in the maternal body, badness of the matter out of which man develops, awful stench, secretion of saliva, urine, and excrement"). Nowadays suffering is always trotted out as the first argument against existence, as its most sinister question. It is well, then, to remember the times when men judged on the opposite principle because they could not do without inflicting suffering, and saw in it a magic of the first order, a veritable bait of seduction to life.
